product.title: Swedish 104 - B2 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from solid B1 to confident B2 Swedish. Each unit pairs a dialogue with an authentic-style text — an email, a news item, a debate excerpt — plus literal glosses of the hard parts, grammar notes, vocabulary with a pronunciation guide, exercises and an answer key. You follow Dian through her master's thesis and first job in Stockholm. The level's real hurdles get a unit each: the field model behind every Swedish sentence, hedging with lär, torde and ska ha, the tiny particles ju, väl and nog, nominal style and officialese, idiomatic particle verbs, counterfactuals, register from SMS slang to debate articles, regional accents and Finland-Swedish, and the art of understatement.

blocks.text: If you have worked through Svenska 103, or reached B1 some other way, you can already live in Swedish: you can rent a room, deal with Skatteverket, survive a job interview and follow a conversation at a dinner table as long as nobody speeds up. What you probably notice now is a different kind of gap. You understand the words, but not always **why** a Swede chose them — why the news says *uppger* and not *säger*, why your colleague answered *Det kan man ju tänka sig* when she clearly meant no, why a perfectly correct sentence of yours still sounds like a translation.

That gap is what B2 is about. Very little of this book is new grammar in the strict sense. Most of it is **choice**: which element to put first in the sentence, when to use the passive and when to say *man*, how strongly to commit to a claim (*det är* · *det verkar* · *det lär* · *det torde*), and which register fits — a text message, an email to your boss, a letter to *Försäkringskassan*, a *debattartikel*. Native speakers make these choices without thinking. This course makes them visible so that you can make them on purpose.

The B2 units also lean much harder on **the small words**. *Ju, väl, nog, då, alltså, liksom* carry attitude — agreement, doubt, impatience, irony — and Swedes use them in nearly every spoken sentence. Leave them out and your Swedish is correct but cold; use them right and people stop switching to English. The same goes for idioms (*ingen ko på isen*), connectors (*å ena sidan … å andra sidan*) and the dry understatement Swedes are famous for.

Two things become harder at this level, and it is better to know it now. First, **real speech is fast**: *ja* for *jag*, *nåt* for *något*, *de e* for *det är*, past tenses clipped to *prata* instead of *pratade*. Second, **not everyone speaks Stockholm Swedish**. You will meet the uvular *r* of Skåne, the singsong of Göteborg, the clipped north, and Finland-Swedish, which has no second tone at all. The pronunciation refresher below and Unit 16 prepare you for both.

The story picks up where Svenska 103 left off. **Dian** is back in Stockholm, writing her master's thesis on sustainable cities, and then starting her first real job at a Stockholm consultancy. **Elin**, **Oskar**, **Ahmad** and Elin's parents **Anna** and **Lars** are still around; new at work is **Mikaela**, a Finland-Swedish colleague from Vasa. Her supervisor **Birgitta** pushes her through draft after draft, the city planner **Johan** gives her an interview, and her fellow student **Viktor** takes the thesis apart as her opponent at the seminars. Once the thesis is handed in come the job ads, an interview full of idioms and, in Unit 16, the first week at work under her new manager **Kristina** — including a client trip to Luleå. After that: a salary negotiation, a night in the archipelago, dinner-table debates about taxes and the climate, an opinion piece for a newspaper — and, at the very end, the wedding of Elin and Erik, where Jonas is toastmaster and Dian has to give a speech.

Twenty units, two texts per unit, about forty minutes per sitting. Take your time with this one: B2 is reached by rereading, listening and writing, not by racing to the last page. *Lycka till* — and enjoy the nuance.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: Units 1–7 rebuild the Swedish sentence at full length — field model, subordinate clauses, aspect, hedging, particles, passive and nominal style. Units 8–14 add the tools of nuance: idiomatic particle verbs, complex prepositions, word formation, argumentation, reported claims, counterfactuals and register. Units 15–20 take it all out into the world: idioms, dialects, the workplace, Swedish society, writing, and a wedding speech. Each unit builds on the ones before it, so work through them in order.

blocks.text: The layout is the one you know from Svenska 101–103, but each unit is longer, so plan on **about forty minutes**, or split a unit over two sittings: the first dialogue and its notes one day, the second text, grammar and exercises the next.
What changes at B2 is how you use each part:

items: **Dialogues and texts** — every unit has two. Often the second one is not a conversation but an authentic-style text: an email, a news article, an official letter, a debate excerpt. Read it once for the gist, then a second time with the notes. Real Swedish texts are rarely read only once.

**Literal gloss** — at this level it covers only the part of the line that is genuinely tricky: a particle verb, a participle phrase, an idiom. If a line has a long gloss, that is your signal that something unusual is happening there.
**Notes** — pay special attention to notes about **tone and register**. At B2, knowing what a sentence means is not enough; you also need to know how it sounds and who would say it.

**Vocabulary** — twenty new words per unit, chosen for B2: abstract nouns, verbs with fixed prepositions, connectors, idioms. Nouns still come with *en* or *ett*, and the "Say it" column still marks stress in CAPITALS.

**Exercises** — more of them ask you to transform rather than fill in: make a sentence more formal, more polite, more hedged, or unpack a heavy nominal sentence into plain Swedish. Do them in writing.
**Answer key** — for transformation exercises, more than one answer can be correct. If yours differs, check whether it says the same thing in the same register.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: Every unit sends you back to an earlier one — often several units back, and sometimes into Svenska 102 or 103. Cover the Swedish, read the English, and rebuild the sentence. At B2, also try a second version: say the same thing more formally, or more casually.
This is how the grammar of earlier levels turns into speed. Don't skip it.

blocks.text: Two new habits for this level. **Shadowing**: play a recording of fast Swedish — a podcast, the news, a TV series — and repeat right after the speaker, matching the melody rather than the words. And **write a little every day**: five sentences about something you read or heard, in the register the topic deserves. B2 is the level where speaking and writing finally pull apart, and both need practice.

You know the sounds of Swedish by now. What B2 adds is the Swedish you actually hear: **fast colloquial speech** and **accents** from outside Stockholm. This page is short on purpose — read it now, then come back to it after Units 14 and 16.
Fast speech: what disappears

In relaxed speech Swedes drop sounds, merge words and clip endings. None of this is sloppy; it is standard spoken Swedish, and you will hear it from teachers, ministers and news anchors off the air. You don't need to copy all of it, but you need to recognize it.

blocks.text: Across word boundaries, *r* still melts into the next sound: *för sent* → **fö-SHENT**, *var snäll* → **vah-SHNEL**. And listen for the **inhaled *ja*** — a short "yes" said while breathing in. It is very common in northern Sweden and in Finland, and it means simple agreement, not surprise.

blocks.title: Finland-Swedish is not a dialect
items: Swedish is one of Finland's two national languages, spoken as a mother tongue by around five percent of the population, mainly along the west and south coasts (Vasa, Helsingfors, Åbo). Its standard form, *finlandssvenska*, is fully correct Swedish with its own pronunciation and a few words of its own — in Finland a *semla* is a plain bread roll, and *kiva* (borrowed from Finnish) means "nice".
Many learners find Finland-Swedish **easier** to understand than Stockholm Swedish: it is slower, clearer and has no tone 2. Your colleague Mikaela in this book speaks it.

blocks.text: The structures of the twenty units in one place. At B2 most of these are not rules you must obey but choices you can make — the tables show what the options are and what each one signals.
The field model: every main clause

Only one element fits in the **fundament**, and the finite verb always comes second. Use the fundament for **known** information or for something you want to contrast; save **new** information for the end of the sentence, where Swedes expect it (Unit 1).
The subordinate clause

No inversion, and *inte*, *aldrig*, *nog*, *verkligen* come **before** the finite verb. An *att*-clause can itself be the subject or object of a sentence: *Att han kom var bra*; *Det var bra att han kom* is the more common, lighter version (Unit 2).

blocks.text: Nominal style and how to unpack it

A participle can carry a whole clause in front of the noun: *den av regeringen föreslagna lagen* = *lagen som regeringen har föreslagit*. Heavy noun chains are typical of *myndighetsspråk*; the plain-language ideal, *klarspråk*, unpacks them into verbs: *Efter genomförandet av utvärderingen …* → *När vi hade utvärderat projektet …* (Units 6–7).

blocks.title: Compound words: one rule
items: The **last** part decides the meaning and the gender: *en stad* → *en storstad*, *ett hus* → *ett hyreshus*. The **first** part carries the main stress. Read long words from the back: *arbets·miljö·verket* = the agency for the environment at work.

blocks.title: Using idioms
items: Recognizing idioms matters more than using them. When you do use one, use it **whole and exactly** — Swedes notice a mangled idiom immediately, and *ingen gris på isen* gets a laugh you didn't plan for.

blocks.text: You have reached the end of B2 — and of the Svenska series. You can follow a news broadcast, argue a point in a meeting without giving offense, read an official letter and answer it in the right register, write a structured opinion piece, recognize the major accents, and stand up at a wedding and make people laugh in Swedish. At B2 you are no longer a learner who sometimes manages; you are a speaker who sometimes makes mistakes.
Three things waiting at C1

items: **Academic and professional writing.** Long, carefully cohesive texts, references, and the precise vocabulary of a field. If you plan to study at a Swedish university in Swedish, the **Tisus** test (*Test i svenska för universitetsstudier*) is the usual proof of level.
**Speed and implicature.** Understanding not only what is said quickly, but what is left unsaid: irony, understatement, the polite *vi får se* that means no.
**Range.** Being able to move between registers at will — a radio debate in the morning, a *fika* joke at three, a formal complaint in the evening — without slipping.

blocks.text: Material at your level now

items: **Sveriges Radio** — *Ekot* for news, *P1* documentaries, and *Språket i P1*, a weekly program where listeners' questions about Swedish are answered by linguists.
**SVT Play** — series and documentaries with Swedish subtitles; switch the subtitles off once a week to test yourself.
**Opinion pages** — *DN Debatt* and the *ledare* (editorials) of the big papers: ideal for studying argumentation and connectors.
**Swedish fiction** — start with contemporary crime or literary novels you already know in translation; knowing the plot frees your attention for the language.

blocks.title: A last note about Swedes
items: At B2, Swedes will mostly stop switching to English — which is a compliment, and also a sign that from now on you will be held to native standards in tone. That is exactly what this book has prepared you for.
And remember the *jantelag*: nobody here will tell you your Swedish is amazing. If someone says **"Du pratar ju riktigt bra svenska"**, with that little *ju*, take it as the highest praise there is.

blocks.text: *Tack för att du har följt Dian hela vägen hit. Skål — och vi hörs!* — Thanks for following Dian all the way here. Cheers — and talk soon!
